meta.title: Photographing Men: Posing, Lighting, and Shooting Techniques for Portrait and Fashion Photography
meta.author: Jeff Rojas

parts.title: A New Perspective on Photographing Men: Techniques for Portrait and Fashion

sentences: This book, "Photographing Men," by Jeff Rojas, provides a **new perspective** on men's portrait, commercial, and fashion photography.
Rojas emphasizes that while there's abundant educational material for photographing women, there's a **lack of information for men**, leading many to believe there's limited creative freedom.
He argues this isn't true, highlighting that **men care about their physical appearance** and that there's a **growing market** for male portraits, especially with the rise of men's fashion.
The book will teach you how to **define a subject's features**, including face and body shapes, and how to **compensate for perceived flaws**.
It also covers **posing techniques** to make subjects look natural, masculine, and confident, various **lighting techniques**, and **post-production methods** to enhance male features.
Rojas stresses the importance of **thinking ahead** before a shoot, considering media, background, subject, attire, light, and lens choice, to ensure professionalism and preparedness.
He also includes a **bonus video** with five go-to poses and considerations for working with male subjects.

parts.title: Mastering Photography for Diverse Face Shapes

sentences: **Photography** involves subjects of **diverse** shapes, sizes, and ages.
As a photographer, you will encounter clients who are tall or short, broad or thin, athletic or less fit, young or old.
It's **crucial** to master capturing these differences so that you are never intimidated by any client.
This guide focuses on identifying unique physical attributes and learning how to **accentuate** them effectively.
It's **unacceptable** to hide subjects due to their physique; instead, you must set aside personal biases and **prioritize** making every subject look their absolute best.
Each man's face is unique, with different **face shapes**.
Your role is to help subjects put their **best face forward** by studying their face shape to make informed choices about **lighting**, **lenses**, and **editing** in Adobe Photoshop.
There are seven basic male face shapes: **square**, **round**, **triangular**, **oblong**, **oval**, **diamond**, and **heart**.
Understanding these shapes helps you select the best techniques to **complement** features and **compensate** for perceived flaws.

For example, with a **square face**, the goal is to make it appear **narrower** and **longer** by darkening the corners and highlighting the forehead and chin, and using **longer lenses** (70mm or more).
For **round faces**, the aim is to make features look **less wide** by darkening the sides and highlighting the forehead and chin, using **smaller, directional light sources** and **longer lenses**.

For **triangular faces**, which are longer than wide with a wide hairline and pointed chin, the objective is to make the forehead look **less wide** and the face **less narrow** by highlighting the forehead's center, chin, and under the eyes, while darkening cheekbones.
Again, **longer lenses** are recommended, and photographing at or slightly below eye level is key to avoiding an exaggerated forehead.

parts.title: Optimizing Facial Features Through Lighting and Lenses

sentences: For **oblong faces**, the goal is to make them look **shorter and broader**.
You can achieve this by **lightening** the face, especially by adding **highlights around the cheeks** using techniques like dodge and burn.
This helps **balance the length and width** of the head and draws attention to key facial features.
Using a **broad, soft light source** and a **reflector** (especially with Rembrandt lighting) on the opposite side can also widen the face.
While **longer lenses (70mm or more)** are generally recommended for proportion, a **wide-angle lens used horizontally** can visually broaden an oblong face.
For **oval faces**, considered ideal and balanced (1.5 times longer than wide), the aim is to **maintain this balance**.
Evenly **highlighting the forehead, cheeks, and chin** with dodge and burn is key.
Using **lenses with minimal distortion**, such as **prime lenses**, is recommended.
It's also important to **reduce any shadows with reflectors** to preserve the face's natural balance.
**Diamond faces**, widest at the temples and cheekbones, benefit from **negative fill** to absorb light from the cheekbones and **accentuating the forehead and chin** to centralize attention.
Dodge and burn can darken cheekbones and highlight the forehead/chin.
**Avoid wide-angle lenses horizontally** as they can exaggerate cheekbone width.
**Heart-shaped faces**, with wider foreheads tapering to a pointy chin, require **reducing forehead width** and **widening the chin** for balance.
This involves **darkening forehead corners and cheekbones** while **highlighting the forehead and chin**.
**Feathering light** slightly off the forehead towards the center face and chin is effective.
**Avoid wide-angle lenses**; **longer lenses (70mm or more)** are preferred to compress the image and maintain proportions.

Finally, choosing the **right lens is crucial** due to **lens distortion**, with **prime lenses** generally being the **best choice for portraits** due to their fixed focal length, sharper images, and less distortion.

parts.title: Face Shapes, Lenses, Contouring, and Body Types in Portrait Photography

sentences: To **find your subject's face shape** for portrait photography, a guide or an online tool like **www.faceplusplus.com** can be used.
This website offers facial recognition to identify celebrity look-alikes, and you can then Google that celebrity's face shape to find your subject's.
For portraits, it's generally best to use **medium focal lengths (50mm to 135mm)** to avoid lens distortion, though distortion can sometimes be used creatively.
For instance, a **vertical wide-angle lens** can subtly **thin a rounder face**.
The author's preferred studio lenses are 50mm, 85mm, and 90mm, while for location shooting, they use 24–70mm and 70–200mm for versatility.
The author discusses **contouring faces** without makeup, applying the concept to men's portrait photography.
Instead of makeup, which can clog pores and remove natural skin textures, they achieve similar results using **lighting techniques or Photoshop editing**.

By strategically using **highlights and shadows**, they can **define features** like cheekbones and jawlines and **guide the viewer's attention** to central facial areas such as the eyes, nose, and lips.
This method doesn't require dramatic lighting and can also be recreated **in-camera** using lighting.
Understanding different **body types** and physiques is crucial for a photographer, even if the older psychological theories linked to them are outdated.
The author focuses on the **chest-to-waist ratio** for accentuating male physiques, aiming to widen shoulders and narrow the waistline, particularly for **ectomorphic (skinny) body types**.

parts.title: Photography Tips for Different Male Body Types

sentences: When photographing **skinnier men**, your goal is to make them appear more **“built”** rather than skinnier.
You can achieve this by making their **shoulders appear wider than their torso**.
Have the subject **face the camera** to add width and ensure proportionality.
Additionally, a **seven-eighths angle**, with the head slightly turned away, can make them look less thin.
It's crucial to minimize **negative space between limbs** to make them appear wider, and avoid **vertical wide-angle lenses** as they can make subjects look skinnier due to distortion.
Photograph at **eye level or slightly above** instead of low angles to maintain proportionality.
Always remember to use **broad light sources** to widen the subject’s face and overall appearance.
For **athletic (mesomorph)** body types, which have a **well-defined chest and broad shoulders**, the goal is to avoid making them look larger or thinner than they are.
These body types are generally **easiest to photograph** due to their natural symmetry.
When photographing **heavier (endomorph)** body types, focus on making their **shoulders appear wider than their torso** and avoid adding to their size.
Position them at a **45-degree angle** instead of straight on to define their shape better.
**Create negative space** between the torso and arms to make the body width appear proportionate.
Shoot from **higher angles** to make the torso appear thinner than the shoulders, and use **longer lenses** (at least 50mm) to compress their shape.
When photographing subjects, **avoid harsh direct sunlight** to prevent large glares on their head, especially at midday.
If an overcast day isn't possible, seek **open or covered shade**.

For backgrounds, choose ones that **don't contrast sharply** with the subject's skin tone; light-skinned subjects on light backgrounds and dark-skinned subjects on dark backgrounds help **focus attention on the face** rather than the head.
To manage features like **hair loss** or **larger than normal features**, use a **shallow depth of field** to blur the top of the head and direct focus to the face.
When selecting lenses, **avoid wider-angle lenses** (like 35mm or 24mm) as they can **distort and elongate features**.
For skin blemishes like **acne, scars, and wrinkles**, soft lighting is key to **reduce their appearance** by minimizing harsh shadows.
Larger, softer light sources are generally better, or use **diffused light outdoors** like open shade or scrims.
Fill cards can also soften harsh shadows indoors.

parts.title: Advanced Photo Editing & Posing Techniques: Rosacea, Double Chins, Gray Hair, and Glasses

sentences: To remove unwanted rosacea or change hair/clothing colors, use a **Hue/Saturation layer**.
Select "Reds" and increase **Saturation to +100** to see affected areas.
Use the slider to feather the red range, isolating desired reds.
Lower Saturation to 0, then subtly increase the slider toward blue to eliminate reddish areas.
Mask unwanted effects with the **Brush tool**.
Even slim people can have a double chin.
To reduce this in-camera, subjects should **stick out their chin** with their **forehead slightly forward**.
Use **short lighting** to define the face and hide the double chin.
Shoot **slightly above eye level** with a **wider aperture**.

parts.title: The Art of Body Language in Photography

sentences: The author, a former salesman, realized the **power of body language** through observing a successful colleague named George.
George **mimicked his clients' body language**, which helped him close deals.
This experience taught the author that understanding nonverbal cues is an **art**, not just a science, and is crucial for an "image maker" to direct subjects to express how they want to be perceived.
In photography, **nonverbal communication is paramount** as people judge based on appearance.
Posing isn't just about accentuating features; a subject's gestures convey strong messages.
For example, **crossed arms** often signal **defensiveness** or **nervousness**, which can be detrimental for professionals like doctors.

The author emphasizes discussing a subject's **personal identity and brand** to influence posing and advises photographers to **educate clients** on the meaning behind poses to achieve the desired perception.
A **reference guide** for **posing men** in **standing positions** focuses on making them look **taller**, **thinner**, and **younger**.
The key is to **accentuate their figure** using **negative space** and **lengthening the body**.
You'll learn that not every pose suits every individual, but with **subtle adjustments**, you can **complement any physique**.
The guide provides **clear descriptions** for each pose, ensuring you can **pose anyone** regardless of their shape or size.

Several specific standing poses are detailed, including **"Hands in Pocket with Feet Shoulder-Width Apart"** for a basic start, **"One Hand on Shoulder, Other Hand in Pocket, with Legs Shoulder-Width Apart"** which involves shifting weight and looking over the shoulder, and **"Hands in Pockets and Legs Apart"** for a 45-degree turn with relaxed shoulders.
The chapter also introduces **"Arms and Legs Crossed"** to thin out the torso and avoid clenched fists, and the crucial concept of **"Forced Perspective"**.

This optical illusion can be used to **advantageously alter perceptions** of size, such as making a stomach appear smaller or broadening shoulders, and emphasizes keeping limbs on the same focal plane to **avoid shortening them** and **elongate the physique**.
When photographing subjects in **seated poses**, it's crucial to make them feel **confident and comfortable** while maintaining **negative space** and **structure** to define their physique.
Be aware of **foreshortening**, where limbs pointed at the camera appear larger; aim to keep limbs **parallel to the background** to **elongate the body**.
For instance, repositioning a leg can prevent it from looking disproportionately shorter.

Addressing the common issue of men having "extra love" around their midsections when sitting, the goal is to either **elongate the body** to extend the skin or use a combination of **styling and posing** to **draw less attention** to this area.
Several poses are discussed, including the natural "Hands Over Legs, Leaning Forward, Facing Camera" pose, emphasizing how **angle and setting** can vary it.
A key tip is to have hands **block the crotch** to avoid distractions.

Other poses involve sitting on a prop with **knees bent** and hands strategically placed to create **negative space**, and another with **one hand in a pocket** and the other on a knee, considering **posture** for different body types.
For crossed-arm and crossed-leg poses, **rotating the subject 90 degrees** can **elongate limbs** and enhance perceived height.
When photographing subjects, **camera angle** significantly impacts their appearance.
For instance, a subject appears **shorter** when parallel to the lens but **taller** when perpendicular to it due to **lens compression**.
To make subjects look more powerful and confident, it's best to photograph them at **eye level or below**, as a high camera angle can make them appear smaller or inferior.
Another important posing tip is to **stretch the body** to reduce the appearance of accumulated skin, especially when subjects are sitting or lying down.
This technique, similar to extending the neck to reduce a double chin, can be applied to various body areas by adjusting the subject's posture.

Inspiration for timeless and effortless poses can be drawn from **16th and 17th-century paintings and sculptures**, particularly those by artists like Michelangelo, known for their masterful understanding of the human form.

parts.title: Achieving the Perfect Fit: Suits and Casual Wear

sentences: A **well-fitted suit** is crucial for a flattering look, ensuring the jacket **hugs the frame**, isn't too tight or loose in the torso, and the pants **don't gather** or have excess material.
Sleeves should hit just below the **wrist bone**, with about **half an inch of shirt cuff showing**.
The jacket length should fall into the hand with curled fingers and **cover the rear**.
Beyond suits, **casual wear** also needs proper fit.
Many men wear clothes that are either too large, making them look bigger, or too small, which is harder to fix than clothes that are slightly too big and can be clipped.
Always **prioritize fit** over subjective fashion.
Additionally, pants should have **one break** at the shoe top, meaning they hang about an inch off the ground without showing socks, and the jacket collar should fit **flat against the neck**.

parts.title: Styling and Lighting Techniques for Men's Photography

sentences: **Backgrounds** are crucial when photographing larger subjects.
**Avoid contrasting colors** that make the subject look bigger; instead, choose a **similar background color** to blend their physique and **focus attention** on their face and arms.
Even with a simple black V-Flat, the goal is to direct focus away from size.
For **taller, skinnier men**, long sleeves or pant legs help, or rolling sleeves to add fabric.
If clothing options are limited, **accessories like hats** can redirect attention.
It's important for skinny men to wear **appropriately fitting clothes**, as baggy attire can make them appear even smaller.
**Avoid large accessories**, opt for **layers** to create the illusion of a larger figure, and choose **lighter solid colors** to widen their appearance.
For **shorter men**, **slim-fitting clothing** and **vertical stripes** can elongate their stature.
Shoes with a **slight heel** add height, but avoid bulky ones.
Wearing **colors without contrast** (like black jeans with black boots) can also make legs appear longer by eliminating visual breaks.
To conceal **double chins or shorter/wider necks**, **V-neck shirts** visually elongate the neck, as do open dress shirts.
Conversely, for **long or skinny necks**, opt for **long-sleeved shirts with wider spread collars** and avoid V-necks or necklaces that draw attention to the neck.
The text then transitions into **lighting men**, emphasizing that the difference between good and bad light is **subjective**.
Commercial and portrait lighting techniques can overlap, with the key distinctions being **creative direction, emotion, production, subject matter, and retouching quality**.
**Lighting techniques** for **portrait photography** involve various setups to achieve different looks.

It starts with **reflective umbrellas**, explaining that they broaden and soften light by reflecting a strobe's flash, and come in white, gold, and silver, with white preferred for smooth skin tones in a studio.
Several specific **portrait lighting styles** exist.
**Rembrandt light** is a basic yet dramatic technique, identifiable by a **triangle of light on the cheek**, achieved by placing the light 45 degrees offset and 45 degrees higher than the subject.
It emphasizes the importance of a **catch light** in the eye and suggests using a **reflector or V-flat** to reduce blemishes and retouching time.
The "Clean Background" setup uses a background softbox to create highlights on the jawline and cheekbones while serving as the background.
"Clean Portrait" is a modified **clamshell lighting** with two beauty lights, creating a dramatic look with sharper light falloff and varying power ratios (e.g., 4:1) for different effects.
A "Dramatic Portrait" setup uses a single main light at 45 degrees down with a 20-degree grid to accentuate cheekbones and jawline, with tips to avoid "lifeless" eyes.
"The Refined Man" is a favorite for fashion editorials, creating drama while lighting the subject's face and attire effectively.

parts.title: Lighting Techniques: Large Parabolic Umbrella and Painterly Portraits

sentences: A setup using a **large parabolic umbrella in Rembrandt position** illuminates both the subject and the background due to its size.
The subject is 5-6 feet from the background, and the light is 3 feet from the subject.
For a softer light, the **Westcott Zeppelin** is recommended with both **inner and outer 1-stop diffusion panels**.

If the Zeppelin is too bulky, a **Profoto Umbrella Deep White L with 1-stop diffusion material** can be used, though it's slightly softer, potentially requiring adjustments like moving the subject or blocking light to avoid lighting the background simultaneously.
A **Painterly Portrait** creates **drama** with a simple setup using **short lighting**.
This technique puts the camera-facing portion of the subject's face in **shadow**, resulting in a **low-key, darker portrait**.
This has a **slimming and flattering effect** for subjects with larger facial features by narrowing the face.
The **main light is placed 30-40 degrees behind and slightly downward** from the subject, providing a subtle wrap-around light on the shoulder and face.
To reduce shadow, a **white fill card, reflector, or white V-Flat** can be added.
The setup looks great in both **black and white and color**.

parts.title: Efficient Lighting for Sports and Catalog Photography

sentences: **Two lights and two strip boxes** are sufficient for photographing athletes and athletic apparel.
This setup allows for creating a **rim light** on equipment (like a soccer ball) while fully illuminating the subject's face by angling the rim lights.

Turning the subject towards one light can create a **long, thin shadow**, adding drama and accentuating features, and can make elements like a soccer ball stand out when surrounded by shadow but highlighted itself.
For catalog photography, especially men's catalogs, a **sweep background** eliminates creases and reduces retouching.
Two background lights are used, placed equally distant, with one offset 30 degrees towards the bottom and the other 30 degrees towards the top, ensuring even lighting from head to feet.
A **Plexiglas surface** provides a reflective base for showcasing items like sneakers and can bounce light to illuminate legs.

A **Profoto Softlight Reflector White ("Beauty Dish")** without a grid can provide enough contrast for texture, wrap around the subject, and light the background, creating a seamless look between the Plexiglas and background.

parts.title: Lighting Techniques for Various Photography Campaigns

sentences: Various **lighting techniques** are used for different photography campaigns, especially for **eyewear, luxury, and fashion**.
For "Eyewear Campaign I," the goal is to draw attention to the **glasses** without catchlights in the eyes.
This is achieved by placing a **beauty dish** with a grid 2 feet overhead to light the area around the subject's eyes.
A second light at minimal power is used in front to fill shadows and illuminate the background.
For "Eyewear Campaign II," the focus is on subtle tones to highlight eyewear.
The **main light** is at 45 degrees (Rembrandt position), 3 feet away, to light the face and create soft tones.
A **rim light** is placed 45 degrees and 3 feet behind, while a white reflector and V-flat help fill shadows and create a small highlight to guide the eye to the cheekbones and temples.
The "Luxury Campaign" uses a **simple single light setup** in Rembrandt position (45 degrees, 4-5 feet from background) to create gradual tones, lighting both the subject and background.
This is effective for accentuating **jewelry and accessories**.
For "Simple Texture," a 47-inch **parabolic umbrella** with diffusion panels provides soft light, while two black V-flats absorb light to enhance texture and define features.
"Natural Light" emphasizes **open shade** for soft, gradual shadows, with light often bouncing off surfaces like concrete.

Finally, "Eyewear Campaign III" demonstrates how to achieve a campaign look with minimal equipment, using a **single speedlight** and a Rogue FlashBender 2 XL Pro to accentuate the subject's face and glasses.
**Post-production** can further enhance details like logos.
